splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over Auer/Kisor deference to agency interpretations when construing ambiguous provisions in the Sentencing Guidelines that impose criminal penalties.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's commentary expanding criminal liability when a Guidelines provision is ambiguous, or whether the rule of lenity should resolve the ambiguity in the defendant's favor. This affects how sentencing enhancements are applied across the federal system.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity prevails over agency deference when construing ambiguous criminal provisions, meaning ambiguity must be resolved in the defendant's favor rather than deferring to the government's interpretation.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference (Auer/Kisor) to the Sentencing Commission's commentary takes precedence over the rule of lenity, allowing the Commission's anti-defendant interpretations to control.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, is entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor when the guideline text does not mention inchoate offenses.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary can authoritatively expand the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include conspiracy and other inchoate offenses not mentioned in the guideline text. This split affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions face significantly enhanced sentences under the career-offender provision.

positions.label: Commentary is authoritative
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is entitled to deference as the Commission's authoritative interpretation, and inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses under the career-offender guideline.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, and the commentary impermissibly expands the definition beyond the guideline's plain language, so conspiracy convictions do not qualify.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any single criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether a defendant must satisfy all three criminal-history disqualifiers in § 3553(f)(1) to be ineligible for safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any one criterion is sufficient. This split leads to dramatically different sentences for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on the circuit in which they are sentenced.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' means 'and,' so defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1).

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any single criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' operates disjunctively, so possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule includes substances not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance underlying a state conviction to also be federally controlled. This split affects whether state drug convictions can serve as predicates for sentencing enhancements, with significant implications for defendants in states with broader drug schedules.

positions.label: No federal-law limitation — state offenses qualify
positions.summary: Holds that 'an offense under state law' in § 4B1.2(b) includes state drug convictions regardless of whether the particular substance is controlled under federal law, finding no textual basis to graft a federal limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Federal-law limitation applies — substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance at issue is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the First Step Act's non-retroactive anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement in U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) permitting such consideration exceeds its statutory authority.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, particularly the First Step Act's elimination of mandatory stacked 25-year sentences under § 924(c), can support a compassionate release motion. Some circuits hold that non-retroactive legal changes can never be considered, while others and the Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment allow them as potential grounds for relief.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and the Sentencing Commission's attempt to say otherwise exceeds its statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's policy statement in § 1B1.13(b)(6).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions or terms of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) must proceed via habeas corpus or may bring civil rights actions, and whether habeas jurisdiction extends to challenges to BOP decisions regarding prerelease custody under the First Step Act.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists over whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for prisoners challenging conditions of confinement, or whether civil rights actions (§ 1983 or Bivens) are also available. The split affects federal prisoners' ability to challenge BOP decisions on matters like earned time credits and prerelease custody transfers under the First Step Act.

positions.label: Habeas available for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus jurisdiction extends to challenges to conditions and terms of confinement, including BOP decisions on prerelease custody, not just challenges to the fact or duration of confinement.

positions.label: Habeas limited to fact/duration of confinement
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus is limited to challenges to the fact or duration of confinement, and conditions-of-confinement claims must be brought as civil rights actions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in asset equity belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether property appreciation that occurs between a Chapter 13 filing and a good-faith conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. This split affects debtors who experience home value appreciation during their Chapter 13 plan and later need to convert to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A) and the broad scope of § 541(a) mean that post-petition appreciation in property value inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure establishes that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtors, not the estate, consistent with the statute's purpose of encouraging good-faith conversions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order is governed by the civil timeline (60 days when the government is a party) or the criminal timeline (14 days).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case or part of the criminal case itself, which determines whether the appellant has 14 or 60 days to file a notice of appeal. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the civil appeal deadline (60 days when the government is a party) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal case, so the shorter criminal appeal deadline (14 days) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose revocation sentences to punish defendants for violations of supervised release, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to promoting the defendant's reentry into society.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether supervised release revocation sentences may serve a punitive purpose. The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to expressly punish defendants for violations, while other circuits hold that revocation sentences must focus on the defendant's successful reintegration into the community, not punishment for the breach itself.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly impose revocation sentences to punish defendants for supervised release violations, placing the Sixth Circuit at the extreme of the circuit split.

positions.label: Punishment is impermissible
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release revocation sentences should not be used to punish the defendant but rather to facilitate reintegration and protect the public.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: This split concerns the timing of actuarial assumption selection for withdrawal liability calculations under ERISA. The outcome affects billions of dollars in potential obligations because the timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, as the statute does not require assumptions to be fixed before that date.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be fixed by the statutory measurement date (end of prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability about potential withdrawal liability.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled during the period a supervisee is a fugitive, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: No tolling — term runs continuously
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release terms run continuously without tolling, and there is no statutory basis for courts to extend the period by judicially creating a fugitive tolling doctrine.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: A 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face the additional gatekeeping requirement of § 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars relitigating any previously presented claim — when bringing successive § 2255 motions. If it applies, federal prisoners face a stricter bar than Congress may have intended, in addition to § 2255(h)'s separate requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement beyond § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, so they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits have disagreed on the standard for evaluating whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The outcome affects whether election rule disputes can be adjudicated before elections or are pushed to post-election litigation, with significant practical implications for election administration nationwide.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge state election laws that allegedly dilute their votes or create competitive injury, allowing pre-election adjudication.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates lack Article III standing to challenge election rules pre-election, requiring a more concrete showing of injury than mere competitive disadvantage.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal court documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: Circuits have not uniformly addressed whether denial of a motion to seal medical records in litigation constitutes a collateral order that is immediately appealable. The D.C. Circuit held that medical privacy is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate review, an approach not universally adopted.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that an order denying a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable because maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of high order that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal does not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements because post-judgment appellate remedies can adequately vindicate the privacy interest.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have diverged on the standards applicable to discrimination claims arising in hospitality and service industry contexts, including questions about liability and remedies. SCOTUS granted cert to resolve the split, indicating the Second Circuit's approach was sufficiently contested.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Adopts broader standards for establishing discrimination liability in hospitality or service establishments, with more expansive remedies available.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Applies more restrictive standards for discrimination claims in business establishments, limiting the scope of liability and available damages.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether state laws categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violate the Equal Protection Clause, and whether as-applied challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits have divided on the constitutionality of state laws that categorically exclude transgender women from women's sports teams, with some recognizing viable as-applied equal protection challenges where individuals have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and others upholding categorical exclusions.

positions.label: Categorical bans may violate Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that categorical bans on transgender women's participation in women's sports may violate the Equal Protection Clause as applied to individuals who have medically mitigated their sex-based biological advantages.

positions.label: Categorical bans survive Equal Protection scrutiny
positions.summary: Holds that state laws categorically restricting sports participation based on biological sex survive intermediate scrutiny and do not violate the Equal Protection Clause.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
